questions.html:
A shortest-path tree (SPT) of a graph $G=(V, E)$ rooted at a source $s$ is a tree in which the path from $s$ to every other vertex is a shortest path in $G$.

Now, consider a graph $G=(V, E)$ with positive edge weights. We run both Dijkstra's algorithm and the Bellman-Ford algorithm from the same source $s$.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.html: Both algorithms always produce the same shortest-path tree.
Both algorithms always produce the same shortest-path distances from the source to every vertex, but the shortest-path trees may be different.
Dijkstra's algorithm may give different shortest-path distances compared to Bellman-Ford.
There exists only one shortest-path tree for a given graph with positive edge weights.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

A -> FALSE  There can be multiple shortest paths to a vertex with the same minimum distance so both algo may choose diffrent edges  from root 
C -> FALSE    For graphs with positive weights, Dijkstra always gives correct shortest distances.Bellman-Ford also gives correct distances.
D - FALSE     There can be multiple shortest paths to a vertex with the same minimum distance

B - TRUE Both algorithms compute correct shortest distances for all vertices

 

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

Scenario: Graph with positive edge weights.

Analysis:

  • Since edge weights are positive, both algorithms are guaranteed to find the correct shortest path distances.

  • Shortest Path Distances: These are unique. So, both algorithms will output the exact same distance values for every vertex.

  • Shortest Path Tree (SPT): If there are multiple paths with the exact same length, the algorithms might pick different parents depending on tie-breaking rules (e.g., vertex ID order, queue implementation). Thus, the trees (the set of edges used) might differ.

Evaluating Options:

  • A. Both always produce the same SPT. (False, ties can lead to differences).

  • B. Both always produce the same shortest-path distances... but the shortest-path trees may be different. (True).

  • C. Dijkstra may give different distances... (False, distances are unique).

  • D. There exists only one SPT... (False, ties allow multiple valid SPTs).

Correct Option: B

options.html: $X$ may no longer be the shortest $s \rightarrow t$ path because the edge weights have changed.
$X$ will still be the shortest $s \rightarrow t$ path since doubling all edge weights preserves the relative ordering of path lengths.
$X$ will remain shortest only if the graph has no cycles.
$X$ will remain shortest only if all original weights are integers.

questions.solution:

Multiplying/dividing scales all path weights equally, so relative order stays the same.
 Adding/subtracting shifts path weights differently depending on the number of edges, so the shortest path may change.

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

Any linear transformation of all weights maintains all relative path lengths, and thus shortest paths will continue to be shortest paths, and more generally all paths will have the same relative ordering. One simple way of thinking about this is unit conversions between kilometers and miles.

Let $\delta(s, v)$ denote the shortest-path distance from source $s$ to vertex $v$. Consider the following statements.
Which of the following is/are TRUE?

options.html: In a weighted directed graph, Dijkstra's algorithm may relax an edge more than once in a graph with a cycle.
In a weighted directed graph $G=(V, E, w)$ with source $s$, if $G$ has a negative-weight cycle anywhere, then Bellman-Ford necessarily computes an incorrect result for some $\delta(s, v)$.
Bellman-Ford works correctly if all negative-weight cycles are unreachable from the source $s$.
Dijkstra's algorithm always produces correct values of $\delta(s, v)$ if the graph has negative-weight edges but no negative-weight cycles.

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

A. Dijkstra's algorithm may relax an edge more than once in a graph with a cycle.

  • True. Dijkstra relaxes all outgoing edges of a vertex when it is extracted. If the graph has cycles, we might not revisit the vertex (if implemented with a visited set), but in standard implementations (like updates in a priority queue), we might update (relax) the distance to a neighbor multiple times before that neighbor is finalized. (Note: It relaxes each edge $(u,v)$ only once when u is processed, but if we consider the whole process, standard Dijkstra visits each node once and relaxes its edges once. However, if the statement implies "updates the value of a destination node," that happens multiple times. The strictest interpretation is that an edge is relaxed exactly once when its source is processed. Let's look at other options for a clearer candidate).

B. If G has a negative-weight cycle... Bellman-Ford necessarily computes an incorrect result...

  • False. Bellman-Ford computes incorrect results (typically $-\infty$) for vertices reachable from the negative cycle. If the negative cycle is in a disjoint component or unreachable from $s$, Bellman-Ford computes correct distances for reachable nodes.

C. Bellman-Ford works correctly if all negative-weight cycles are unreachable from the source s.

  • True. This is a known property. The algorithm is unaffected by cycles it cannot reach.

D. Dijkstra's algorithm always produces correct values... if graph has negative-weight edges but no negative cycles.

  • False. Dijkstra is greedy. It assumes that once a node is visited, its distance is optimal. A negative edge later in the graph can violate this assumption, leading to incorrect results even without a negative cycle.

Correct Option: C is the unambiguously true statement.

OPTION :- C

questions.html: Suppose a directed graph has no negative cycles. You run the Bellman-Ford algorithm from a source $S$. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: The shortest-path distances from $S$ are always the same, no matter the order of edge relaxations.
The exact shortest-path tree chosen is always the same, no matter the order of edge relaxations.
If a vertex can be reached by two different shortest paths of equal length, the chosen path may depend on relaxation order.
If each vertex has exactly one shortest path from $S$, then the shortest-path tree will not depend on the relaxation order.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Scenario: Directed graph with no negative cycles.

Analysis:

  • A. The shortest-path distances... are always the same...

    • Correct. Shortest path distances are a mathematical property of the graph. As long as there are no negative cycles, the distance is well-defined and unique. Bellman-Ford is guaranteed to find this unique distance regardless of relaxation order.

  • B. The exact shortest-path tree chosen is always the same...

    • Incorrect. If there are multiple paths with the same minimum length, the algorithm might pick one or the other depending on the order in which edges are relaxed.

  • C. If a vertex can be reached by two different shortest paths... chosen path may depend on relaxation order.

    • Correct. (This is the complement of statement B).

  • D. If each vertex has exactly one shortest path... shortest-path tree will not depend on relaxation order.

    • Correct. If the path is unique, the algorithm has no choice but to converge on that single specific tree.

Correct Option: A, C, and D are correct.

 

Official discussion page

questions.html:
Recall the update operation on distances in the Bellman-Ford algorithm:
$$
\operatorname{update}(u \rightarrow v): \quad \operatorname{dist}[v]=\min (\operatorname{dist}[v], \operatorname{dist}[u]+\ell(u, v))
$$
Consider the following graph:
$$
S \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow B
$$
If all edge weights are positive, which is the shortest sequence of update operations that ensures all distances from $S$ are correctly computed, irrespective of the edge weights?

options.html: $A \rightarrow B, S \rightarrow A$
$S \rightarrow A, A \rightarrow B$
$S \rightarrow A$ only
$A \rightarrow B, S \rightarrow A, S \rightarrow B$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

The update operation is: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + l(u, v))

This operation can only find the final shortest-path distance for v if the distance to the previous node, dist[u], is already correct.

S → A → B
We start with dist[S] = 0. All other distances are initialized to infinity: dist[A] = ∞, dist[B] = ∞.  The only path to A is S → A. To calculate dist[A], we must use the update(S → A) operation. This requires dist[S] to be correct (which it is, at 0). The only path to B is S → A → B. To calculate dist[B] using the update(A → B) operation, we must have the correct value for dist[A].

Answer: B

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

 

🔹 The Question Setup

We have a directed graph:

S → A → B

All edges have positive weights.
Let’s denote them as:

  • weight(S → A) = w₁

  • weight(A → B) = w₂

We want to know:

What is the shortest sequence of edge relaxations that ensures all shortest distances from S are correctly computed, no matter what the weights are?

💡 Step 1: Recall the Bellman–Ford update rule

For each edge ( u \to v ):
[
\text{dist}[v] = \min(\text{dist}[v], \text{dist}[u] + w(u, v))
]

That means we use the current knowledge of dist[u] to try to improve dist[v].

But — this only works if dist[u] is already correct (or at least smaller than before).

So, information (shortest distance) flows from source → outward, one edge at a time.

🌱 Step 2: Start from what we know

Initially:

dist[S] = 0
dist[A] = ∞
dist[B] = ∞

The source (S) is the only vertex whose distance is known correctly at the start.

⚙️ Step 3: Propagation of shortest path info

To get the correct distance for A:

  • We must relax the edge S → A.

Then:

dist[A] = min(∞, dist[S] + w₁)
dist[A] = 0 + w₁ = w₁

✅ Now we know the true shortest distance to A.

To get the correct distance for B,
we need the value of dist[A] (because A lies between S and B).

So next, we relax A → B:

dist[B] = min(∞, dist[A] + w₂)
dist[B] = w₁ + w₂

✅ Now we know the true shortest distance to B.

🧩 Step 4: Understanding the dependency chain

Let’s think in terms of information flow:

S → A → B

  • To compute A’s shortest distance, we depend on S.

  • To compute B’s shortest distance, we depend on A (which depends on S).

So the relaxation order must “respect” this dependency.

That means:
[
S \to A \text{ must come before } A \to B
]

Otherwise, B would get updated based on an incorrect (infinite) value of A.

⚡ Step 5: Check each option intuitively

Option A: A → B, S → A

❌ Wrong.

If we relax A → B first:

  • dist[A] is still ∞

  • So dist[B] doesn’t get updated.

Then after S → A, A becomes correct — but B remains outdated.

We’d need another relaxation on A → B → Not the shortest sequence.

Option B: S → A, A → B

✅ Correct.

1️⃣ Relax S → A:
Now A has correct distance.
2️⃣ Relax A → B:
Now B gets its correct distance.

Done! All distances are now correct — with the shortest possible 2 relaxations.

Option C: S → A only

❌ Wrong.

B never gets updated.
dist[B] stays ∞.

Option D: A → B, S → A, S → B

❌ Unnecessary relaxations — we already get everything done with Option B.

✅ Final Answer:

Option B — (S → A, A → B)
is the shortest sequence that guarantees all distances from S are computed correctly, for any positive weights.

🌟 Intuitive Summary

Bellman–Ford’s correctness depends on the order of dependency —
you can think of it as wavefront propagation from the source outward.

For the path:

S → A → B

The correct information flow order is the same as a topological order of edges:
[
(S → A) \text{ before } (A → B)
]

That ensures each node’s shortest path is finalized before its children are relaxed.

💎 GATE-level Insight

This is why Bellman–Ford (and DAG shortest path) can often be optimized:

  • In general, you relax all edges |V|−1 times.

  • But if you relax edges in topological order (like in this example),
    you need only one pass! 🚀

🔚 Key takeaway

ConceptMeaning
Relaxation order mattersYou must relax an edge only after the source node’s distance is correct
In chain graph S→A→BRelax S→A first, then A→B
Relation to topological orderWorks perfectly for acyclic graphs (DAGs)

Would you like me to show how this idea generalizes to a larger DAG (e.g., S→A→B→C→D) — where only one linear pass (topological order) gives all shortest paths instantly?
That’s one of the most elegant insights about Bellman–Ford vs DAG shortest path.

questions.html:
The Bellman-Ford algorithm starts from a source $s$ and repeatedly relaxes all edges.
Consider the following two statements:

($1$) If the graph $G$ has at most $k$ negative-weight edges (anywhere in the graph), then running BellmanFord for only $k$ iterations is enough to compute all shortest path distances from $s$.

($2$) If every shortest path from $s$ to any vertex uses at most $k$ edges, then running Bellman-Ford for $k$ iterations is enough to compute all shortest path distances from $s$.

Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Both ($1$) and ($2$) are true
($1$) is true, ($2$) is false
($1$) is false, ($2$) is true
Both ($1$) and ($2$) are false

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

($1$) False: Even if there are at most $k$ negative edges (anywhere in the graph), this does not limit the required iterations. A path of length $2 k$ with no negative edges still needs $2 k$ relaxations.

($2$) True: If all shortest paths use at most $k$ edges, then after $k$ iterations Bellman-Ford will compute the correct distances.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Statement (1): "If the graph $G$ has at most $k$ negative-weight edges... then running BellmanFord for only $k$ iterations is enough..."

  • Status: False.

  • Reason: The number of iterations required by Bellman-Ford depends on the maximum number of edges in a shortest path, not specifically on the count of negative edges. Even with just one negative edge, a shortest path could traverse many positive edges before or after it. If the shortest path has length $|V|-1$, you need $|V|-1$ iterations to propagate the correct distance, regardless of how many edges are negative.

Statement (2): "If every shortest path from $s$ to any vertex uses at most $k$ edges, then running Bellman-Ford for $k$ iterations is enough..."

  • Status: True.

  • Reason: This is the fundamental property of the Bellman-Ford algorithm. After $i$ iterations, the algorithm correctly computes the shortest path distances for all paths that use at most $i$ edges. If the true shortest path to any node uses at most $k$ edges, then after $k$ iterations, the algorithm will have found it.

Correct Option: C. (1) is false, (2) is true

 

Official discussion page

Given an undirected, unweighted, connected graph G , suppose we run a DFS on G starting at some node s . We find that the DFS tree has the property that for any vertex v , the path in the DFS tree from s to v is a shortest (fewest number of edges) path from s to v in G. 

Which of the following is necessarily true?

options.html: G must be a tree.
G must be acyclic, but not necessarily connected.
G may contain cycles.
DFS always produces the shortest paths in any connected graph.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

DFS produces shortest paths from the root to all vertices iff the graph is a tree.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

For DFS to still produce shortest paths:

  • DFS must never go “too deep” when a shorter route exists

  • That means:
    there cannot exist a shortcut edge that DFS ignores initially

In other words:

DFS must have no opportunity to take a longer path when a shorter one exists

Only a Tree can force DFS to take exactly one path, as there are no alternative paths.

questions.html:
Consider the following statements about shortest paths in graphs:

$1$. In a strongly connected directed graph with integer edge weights, it is possible that there exist vertices $s$ and $t$ such that no shortest path from $s$ to $t$ exists.

$2$. In a graph with positive edge weights, if all edge weights are distinct, then the shortest path between any two vertices $s$ and $t$ is unique.

Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Only statement $1$ is true.
Only statement $2$ is true.
Both statements $1$ and $2$ are true.
Both statements $1$ and $2$ are false.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

Statement 1 is TRUE: The phrase "integer edge weights" allows for negative weights. If a negative-weight cycle is reachable on a path from s to t, the path cost can be made infinitely small. Therefore, no finite shortest path exists.

Statement 2 is FALSE: Just because the individual edge weights are distinct (like 1, 5, 6, 2) doesn't mean their sums can't be equal. Two different paths can have combinations of distinct weights that add up to the same total minimum value (e.g., Path A: 1 + 6 = 7; Path B: 5 + 2 = 7).

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Based on the analysis of the two statements, here is the step-by-step solution:

 

Statement 1 Analysis

 

"In a strongly connected directed graph with integer edge weights, it is possible that there exist vertices $s$ and $t$ such that no shortest path from $s$ to $t$ exists."

  • True.

  • Reason: While a strongly connected graph ensures that there is always a path from $s$ to $t$, the phrase "integer edge weights" allows for negative weights.

  • If the graph contains a negative weight cycle (a cycle where the sum of edges is negative), you can traverse this cycle infinitely many times to make the path weight arbitrarily small (approaching $-\infty$).

  • In such cases, the concept of a "shortest path" becomes undefined because for any path you pick, there exists a longer path with a smaller total weight. Since the graph is strongly connected, this negative cycle affects paths between all pairs of vertices. Thus, no defined shortest path exists.

 

Statement 2 Analysis

 

"In a graph with positive edge weights, if all edge weights are distinct, then the shortest path between any two vertices $s$ and $t$ is unique."

  • False.

  • Reason: Having distinct individual edge weights does not prevent the sum of weights along two different paths from being equal.

  • Counter-Example:

    • Imagine a graph with 3 vertices: $s$, $u$, and $t$.

    • Edge $(s, t)$ has weight 5.

    • Edge $(s, u)$ has weight 2.

    • Edge $(u, t)$ has weight 3.

    • All edge weights $\{2, 3, 5\}$ are distinct and positive.

    • Path 1: $s \to t$ has a total cost of 5.

    • Path 2: $s \to u \to t$ has a total cost of $2 + 3 =$ 5.

    • Both paths have the same minimum cost, so the shortest path is not unique, even though all edge weights are distinct.

 

Conclusion

 

  • Statement 1 is True.

  • Statement 2 is False.

Therefore, the correct option is:

A. Only statement 1 is true.

questions.html:
The figure above shows an undirected graph. Dijkstra's algorithm is being run from source s.

Edges already in the current shortest-path tree are drawn solid; the remaining edges are dashed.

Which dashed edge will be added next to the shortest-path tree by Dijkstra's algorithm?

options.html: Edge (s, v1) with weight 7
Edge (v1, v2) with weight 3
Edge (v6, v7) with weight 3
Edge (v2, v3) with weight 2

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

From the figure, the solid edges already in the shortest-path tree are:

  • $s \rightarrow v 5$ with weight 1

 

  • $v 5 \rightarrow v 6$ with weight 1

 

  • $v 5 \rightarrow v 2$ with weight 2

 

  • $v 2 \rightarrow v 3$ with weight 1


So far, the shortest-path distances are:

  • $d(s)=0$

 

  • $d(v 5)=1$

 

  • $d(v 6)=d(v 5)+1=2$

 

  • $d(v 2)=d(v 5)+2=3$

 

  • $d(v 3)=d(v 2)+1=4$


Now check the dashed frontier edges:

  • ( $\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{v} 1$ ) with weight $7 \rightarrow$ tentative distance $=0+7=7$

 

  • ( $\mathrm{v} 1, \mathrm{v} 2$ ) with weight $3 \rightarrow$ tentative distance $=3+3=6$

 

  • (v6, v7) with weight $3 \rightarrow$ tentative distance $=2+3=5$

 

  • ( $\mathrm{v} 2, \mathrm{v} 3$ ) with weight $2 \rightarrow$ already in the tree, ignore


The smallest tentative distance is from ( $\mathbf{v 6}, \mathbf{v 7}$ ) with total distance $5$.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Based on the Dijkstra's algorithm simulation on the provided graph:

  1. Identify the current state:

    The problem states that solid edges are already in the shortest-path tree (SPT). Let's determine the visited vertices and their shortest path distances from the source s based on these solid edges:

    • s: Distance = 0

    • v5: Connected via (s, v5) with weight 1. Distance $d[v5] = 0 + 1 = \mathbf{1}$.

    • v6: Connected via (v5, v6) with weight 1. Distance $d[v6] = d[v5] + 1 = 1 + 1 = \mathbf{2}$.

    • v2: Connected via (v5, v2) with weight 2. Distance $d[v2] = d[v5] + 2 = 1 + 2 = \mathbf{3}$.

    • v3: Connected via (v2, v3) with weight 1. Distance $d[v3] = d[v2] + 1 = 3 + 1 = \mathbf{4}$. (Note: The path via v6 would be $2+4=6$, so the path via v2 is indeed shorter).

    So, the set of vertices already in the SPT is {s, v5, v6, v2, v3}.

  2. Evaluate candidate edges for the next step:

    Dijkstra's algorithm always picks the "dashed" edge that connects a vertex in the SPT to a vertex outside the SPT such that the total distance from the source is minimized. The unvisited vertices are v1, v4, and v7.

    Let's calculate the potential distance for each unvisited neighbor:

    • To reach v1:

      • Via edge (s, v1) (weight 7): Distance = $d[s] + 7 = 0 + 7 = 7$.

      • Via edge (v2, v1) (weight 3): Distance = $d[v2] + 3 = 3 + 3 = 6$.

      • Minimum distance to v1 is 6.

    • To reach v4:

      • Via edge (v3, v4) (weight 2): Distance = $d[v3] + 2 = 4 + 2 = \mathbf{6}$.

    • To reach v7:

      • Via edge (v6, v7) (weight 3): Distance = $d[v6] + 3 = 2 + 3 = \mathbf{5}$.

      • (Note: v4 is not visited yet, so we cannot use the edge (v4, v7)).

  3. Select the minimum:

    Comparing the best distances to all reachable unvisited nodes:

    • $v1: 6$

    • $v4: 6$

    • $v7: 5$

    The minimum distance is 5. The algorithm will select vertex v7 next. The edge that provides this minimum distance is (v6, v7).

  4. Check the options:

    • A. Edge (s, v1) with weight 7: Incorrect.

    • B. Edge (v1, v2) with weight 3: Incorrect (result distance 6).

    • C. Edge (v6, v7) with weight 3: Correct (result distance 5).

    • D. Edge (v2, v3) with weight 2: Incorrect. This edge is already solid (part of the tree), and its weight in the diagram is 1, not 2.

Correct Answer: C. Edge (v6, v7) with weight 3

questions.html:
The Bellman-Ford algorithm is used to compute single-source shortest paths in a directed weighted graph $G=\mathrm{(V, E)}$ with integer edge weights.

In each iteration, it relaxes all edges, but the order in which the edges are relaxed may vary from one iteration to another. For example, in one iteration the algorithm may relax edges in the order $\left(e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}, \ldots\right)$, while in another iteration it may relax them in a completely different order.

Which of the following statements are correct?

options.html: The correctness of the Bellman-Ford algorithm does not depend on the order of edge relaxations in each iteration.
After $k$ iterations, the algorithm guarantees the correct shortest-path distance for all vertices whose shortest path uses at most $k$ edges (anywhere in the graph).
Running fewer than $|V|-1$ iterations may still compute all correct distances if the longest shortest path in the graph uses fewer than $|V|-1$ edges.
The correctness of the Bellman-Ford algorithm depends on the order of edge relaxations in each iteration, i.e., in each iteration, the order of relaxation must be the same as in the first iteration.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Assuming there are no negative-weight cycles reachable from the source:

  1. The correctness of Bellman–Ford does not depend on the order of edge relaxations in each iteration. — True.
    The algorithm will find correct shortest distances after enough iterations regardless of the order you relax the edges (orders can change intermediate values but not the final result after enough rounds).

  2. After k iterations, the algorithm guarantees the correct shortest-path distance for all vertices whose shortest path uses at most k edges. — True.
    This is a standard invariant: after k full passes of relaxing all edges, every shortest path that uses ≤k edges is discovered.

  3. Running fewer than ∣V∣−1 iterations may still compute all correct distances if the longest shortest path in the graph uses fewer than ∣V∣−1| edges. — True.
    If the maximum number of edges on any shortest path from the source is d<∣V∣−1, then d iterations suffice.

  4. The correctness depends on the order of edge relaxations — the order must be the same as in the first iteration. — False.
    There is no need to keep the same order across iterations; any order (even different each iteration) works.

In second option, I get confused as the line: After k iterations, the algorithm guarantees the correct shortest-path distance for all vertices whose shortest path uses at most k edges. looks incomplete because it doesn’t explicitly say “from the source.”

But in Bellman-Ford, whenever we talk about “shortest path” without mentioning anything else, it always means shortest path from the source node, because the algorithm itself is a single-source shortest path algorithm.

questions.html:
There are $n$ magic portals in a game.

  • If you enter portal $i$, it can send you to portal $j$.
     
  • Your power gets multiplied by $T[i][j]$.

Thus, if you follow a sequence of portals
$$
i_{1} \rightarrow i_{2} \rightarrow i_{3} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow i_{k} \rightarrow i_{1},
$$
then the final power is
$$
P=T\left[i_{1}\right]\left[i_{2}\right] \cdot T\left[i_{2}\right]\left[i_{3}\right] \cdots \cdots T\left[i_{k}\right]\left[i_{1}\right] .
$$
We want to check if there exists a cycle of portals such that the final power $P>1$.

We want to somehow use the Bellman-Ford algorithm feature of detecting negative cycles here. We will say: if there is a negative cycle, then final power $P>1$.

For this, we must define the edge weight $w(i, j)$ for each directed edge $(i \rightarrow j)$. Which of the following definitions is correct?

options.html: $w(i, j)=T[i][j]$
$w(i, j)=-T[i][j]$
$w(i, j)=\log (T[i][j])$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

Take option D:
$$
w(i, j)=-\log (T[i][j]) .
$$

In Bellman-Ford, when we go around a cycle, we add weights.

So for a cycle, the total weight becomes:
$$
-\log (T[i][j] \cdot T[j][k] \cdot T[k][i]) .
$$

  • If this value is negative, then

$$
\log (T[i][j] \cdot T[j][k] \cdot T[k][i])>0 .
$$

  • And if $\log$ is positive, it means the product is greater than 1.


In other words:

  • If the product is just a fraction (< 1 ), log is negative

 

  • If the product is $>1$, $\log$ is positive.


So, a negative cycle in Bellman-Ford means the product > 1, i.e. your power increases after the cycle.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Answer is D
Understanding the Problem

In this game, every time we move through a portal, our power is multiplied by the value on that edge. If we complete a cycle, the final power is the product of all the edge values in that cycle:

$$P = T[i_1][i_2] \cdot T[i_2][i_3] \cdots T[i_k][i_1]$$

We want to know if there is a cycle where the power increases, which means

$$P > 1.$$


Why We Cannot Use the Edge Values Directly

The question asks us to use the Bellman-Ford algorithm. The problem is that Bellman-Ford works by adding edge weights, not multiplying them.

If we use the original values $T[i][j]$, the algorithm will only calculate their sum, but our condition depends on their product. So, we need a way to convert multiplication into addition.


Using Logarithms

Logarithms help because they change multiplication into addition:

$$\log(a \cdot b) = \log(a) + \log(b).$$

If we replace every edge weight with its logarithm, then the sum of the edge weights around a cycle becomes

$$\log(P).$$

Our original condition is

$$P > 1.$$

Taking the logarithm of both sides gives

$$\log(P) > \log(1).$$

Since $\log(1) = 0$,

$$\log(P) > 0.$$

So after applying logarithms, we are looking for a cycle whose total weight is greater than zero, i.e., a positive cycle.


Why This Still Does Not Work

Bellman-Ford is designed to find the shortest paths. It can detect negative cycles, but it does not detect positive cycles.

A positive cycle only increases the total path cost, so the algorithm simply ignores it. On the other hand, a negative cycle keeps reducing the path cost, so Bellman-Ford can recognize that something is wrong and reports its existence.

Since our cycle has a positive sum, we need to convert it into a negative one.

 

Converting It into a Negative Cycle

Starting from

$$\log(P) > 0,$$

multiply both sides by $-1$. Remember that multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality:

$$-\log(P) < 0.$$

Now define the weight of each edge as

$$w(i, j) = -\log(T[i][j]).$$

With this change, any cycle that increases the player's power becomes a negative-weight cycle. Bellman-Ford can detect this negative cycle, allowing us to determine whether such a power-increasing cycle exists.

 

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

What is actually happening in the game?

  • You go through portals

  • Each portal multiplies your power

  • After a cycle, your power becomes:

\[P = T[i_1][i_2] × T[i_2][i_3] × ... × T[i_k][i_1]\]
 
If there is a negative cycle then $P>1$,
\[ P>1\]
\[ T[i_1][i_2] × T[i_2][i_3] × ... × T[i_k][i_1]>1\]
 
We want to detect this negative cycle.
 
However in this example every time we cycle the power increases(multiplied)
 
Bellman Ford can only detect a negative cycle if there is a decrease(we something that is negative, so that in Vth iteration there is another relaxation)
 
To achieve this negative behavior we can apply -log to convert the product to a sum that yields a negative results.
\[w(i,j) = -log(T[i][j])\]
 
\[ -log(T1) + -log(T2) + ... > -log(1) \]
 
Example:
Suppose a cycle leads to $2 × 0.5 × 2 = 2 > 1$ (negative cycle)
 
For Bellman Ford to detect this, we apply $-log$ 
 
$-log(2) -log(0.5) -log(2)$
 
$≈ -0.69 +0.69 -0.69 = -0.69$ (negative result that will cause some decrease)

 
Why other options are wrong:
+log will create +ve weight cycles which Bellman-Ford can't detect
Using T or −T does not convert multiplication into addition, so Bellman–Ford cannot reason about the cycle.

questions.html:
Consider a weighted directed acyclic graph (DAG) $G=(V, E, w)$.

  • Edges leaving the source $s$ may have negative weights.
     
  • All other edges are non-negative.

We want to compute shortest path distances $\delta(s, t)$ for all vertices $t$.

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: Dijkstra's algorithm may fail since negative weights are present.
Dijkstra's algorithm always works in graphs with negative edges as long as there is no negative cycle.
Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly in this case.
If a negative edge goes beyond the source (i.e., not directly from $s$ ), then Dijkstra can fail in this DAG.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

Normally, Dijkstra fails with negative edges because it assumes that once a vertex is chosen with the smallest distance, that distance will never change. A negative edge later in the graph can reduce that distance, breaking the algorithm.

In this problem, the graph is a DAG where the only negative edges are directly from the source. All other edges are non-negative.

When Dijkstra starts, it relaxes all edges from the source in the very first step. So even if some of them are negative, the correct shortest distances to those immediate neighbors are already discovered. After this, all further relaxations involve only non-negative edges. Since no later edge can reduce an already finalized distance, Dijkstra's greedy strategy works fine.

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

The correct statements are C and D.

Here is the detailed analysis for each option:

  • A. Dijkstra's algorithm may fail since negative weights are present.

    • FALSE. As analyzed previously, the specific structure of this graph (negative edges only at the source) guarantees that Dijkstra's greedy choice will never be invalidated later in the traversal. Once a node is pulled from the priority queue, its distance is optimal because no future edge can reduce the path length further (all subsequent edges are non-negative).

  • B. Dijkstra's algorithm always works in graphs with negative edges as long as there is no negative cycle.

    • FALSE. This is a very common misconception.

      • Bellman-Ford works as long as there is no negative cycle.

      • Dijkstra requires no negative edges at all (generally). Even without a cycle, a simple negative edge can break Dijkstra.

      • Counter-example: $S \to A (5)$, $S \to B (10)$, $A \to B (-10)$.

      • Dijkstra extracts $A(5)$ then $B(10)$. It finalizes $B$ with distance 10. It never sees that going $S \to A \to B$ costs $5 - 10 = -5$.

  • C. Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly in this case.

    • TRUE. Since all negative weights are attached to the source $S$, they are processed in the very first initialization step. All subsequent relaxations involve non-negative edges. Because path costs can only increase or stay equal after the first step, the first time a node is extracted from the priority queue, it is guaranteed to have reached its global minimum distance.

  • D. If a negative edge goes beyond the source (i.e., not directly from $s$), then Dijkstra can fail in this DAG.

    • TRUE. This statement presents a hypothetical condition ("If...").

    • It essentially asks: "Is the condition 'edges are non-negative' crucial?"

    • Yes. If we allow negative edges deeper in the graph (not just at the source), we return to the general case of Dijkstra with negative edges. As shown in the counter-example for option B, Dijkstra can fail in such scenarios. Therefore, this statement is logically correct.

 

Conclusion

 

The correct options are C and D.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Given

We have a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph).

Conditions:

  1. Edges directly leaving source sss may be negative.
  2. Every other edge is non-negative.

We must determine whether Dijkstra works.

Key Recall About Dijkstra

Dijkstra fails when:

  • a node is finalized too early,
  • and later a shorter path is found through a negative edge.

This happens because Dijkstra assumes:

w(u,v)≥0w(u,v) \ge 0w(u,v)≥0

for all edges.

Important Observation Here

The ONLY negative edges are from the source sss.

So when Dijkstra starts:

  • it immediately relaxes all outgoing edges from sss,
  • including negative ones.

After this:

  • all remaining edges are non-negative,
  • so distances can only increase normally.

No later “surprise shorter path” can appear through hidden negative edges.

Thus Dijkstra still works correctly here.

 

 

Check Options

A

Dijkstra may fail since negative weights are present.

❌ False

Negative edges alone do not necessarily break Dijkstra here.

B

Dijkstra always works with negative edges if no negative cycle.

❌ False

Dijkstra can fail even without negative cycles.

C

Dijkstra works correctly in this case.

✅ TRUE

D

If a negative edge appears beyond source, Dijkstra can fail.

✅ This statement is also true generally.

But the question asks the correct statement about THIS setting.

  • Initialize: $d(S)=0$. After removing $S$, neighbors have


$d(A)=3 \mathrm{via}(S, A), d(C)=1 \mathrm{via}(S, C), d(D)=4 \mathrm{via}(S, D)$.
(Others $=\infty$.)
 

  • 1st deleted after $S: C$ (distance 1) - via $(S, C)$.


Relax edges out of $C$ :

$C \rightarrow D: 1+5=6$ (no update, since $d(D)=4$ );

$C \rightarrow F: 1+8=9 \Rightarrow d(F)=9$ via $(C, F)$.
 

  • 2nd deleted: $A$ (distance 3) - via $(S, A)$.


Relax: $A \rightarrow B: 3+7=10 \Rightarrow d(B)=10$ via $(A, B)$.
$A \rightarrow D: 3+9=12$ (no update).
 

  • 3rd deleted: $D$ (distance 4 ) - via ( $S, D$ ).


Relax: $D \rightarrow G: 4+13=17 \Rightarrow d(G)=17 ; D \rightarrow E: 4+14=18 \Rightarrow d(E)=18$.
 

  • 4th deleted: $F$ (distance 9 ) - via ( $C, F$ ).

(After deleting $D$ the smallest remaining distance is $F=9$, then $B=10$, etc.)

Thus the four deleted vertices (in order) and their connecting edges are:

C via ( $S, C$ ), $A$ via ( $S, A$ ), D via ( $S, D$ ), $F$ via ( $C, F$ ) - option D.

questions.html:
Consider a directed graph $G=(V, E)$ with non-negative edge weights. Let $S$ be a source vertex.

$S1$. If $S \rightarrow a \rightarrow b$ is a shortest path from $S$ to $b$, then both subpaths $S \rightarrow a$ and $a \rightarrow b$ are also shortest paths.

$S2$. If $S \rightarrow u$ is a shortest path from $S$ to $u$, and $u \rightarrow v$ is a shortest path from $u$ to $v$, then the concatenated path $S \rightarrow u \rightarrow v$ is necessarily a shortest path from $S$ to $v$.

Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Both $S 1$ and $S 2$ are true.
$S 1$ is true; $S 2$ is false.
$S 1$ is false; $S 2$ is true.
Both $S1$ and $S2$ are false.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

  • S1 is true: Shortest paths have the optimal substructure property. Any subpath of a shortest path is itself a shortest path.

 

  • S2 is false: Two shortest paths do not always combine into another shortest path.


Counterexample for $S 2$ :

Edges:

  • $S \rightarrow u=5$

 

  • $u \rightarrow v=5$

 

  • $S \rightarrow v=6$


Here:

  • $S \rightarrow u$ is shortest to $u$.

 

  • $\quad u \rightarrow v$ is shortest to $v$ from $u$.

 

  • But $S \rightarrow u \rightarrow v=10$, while the direct edge $S \rightarrow v=6$ is shorter.


So $S \rightarrow u \rightarrow v$ is not the shortest path from $S$ to $v$.
